extracted.intended_audience: PR and communications professionals responsible for press releases and earned-media campaigns
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, creating, and distributing multimedia assets (photos, video, infographics, embeds, audio) to support press releases and earned-media outreach. Emphasizes tying multimedia to messaging, newsroom habits, and distribution to maximize journalist uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia must be strategic and integrated, not an afterthought
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia should not be treated as an afterthought in the PR planning process; visual content must connect innately to the text and other elements in a press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create multimedia as part of the story’s foundation rather than tacked on at the end. Ensure visuals, audio and text reinforce the same messaging and objectives. Avoid generic or dull content—multimedia should meaningfully advance the story and be conceived early in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia should capture attention and compete with social content
rubrics_metrics.description: Because journalists and audiences increasingly consume short-form, visually-driven content (Stories, short video), multimedia for PR needs to be accessible, inventive, and able to capture attention quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assets that are quick to comprehend and shareable; think about 15-second story formats and lightweight production approaches. Prioritize creativity and accessibility to stand out amid high competition for influencers’ attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists want ready-to-use graphics and video
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters working to tight deadlines prefer pitches that include ready-to-use multimedia (images, video) so they don’t have to source or edit assets themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach images and videos directly to pitches; avoid forcing journalists to source or reformat your assets. Providing complete, properly formatted assets increases the chance of pickup and future trust from the reporter (Fratti quote / Forbes reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Storyboard the news or campaign from start to finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Walk through the story the way a director lays out a film: plan how multimedia will support each release and stage of a campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide number of releases, which multimedia assets are unique vs repurposed, what will 'show' rather than 'tell' (e.g., video summarizing a white paper), and which assets must be created in advance vs captured on the fly (e.g., event photography needing fast turnaround). Use this planning to allocate resources and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the market’s multimedia storytelling habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Research target outlets to learn how they use third-party multimedia: where they place videos/images, whether they edit supplied material, what platforms they publish to and how they annotate shared assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at representative samples of target outlets and ask editors about preferences. Note whether they embed raw video, edit clips into B-roll, write their own captions, repurpose audio for podcasts, or share via social channels. Use findings to tailor asset format, timing, and packaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect multimedia with subject matter expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure subject matter experts (SMEs) know exactly what multimedia will be disseminated and are prepared to elaborate on what isn’t shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do media training/prep that covers unanswered questions multimedia might raise; ensure SMEs are comfortable with the content. Include call-to-actions in multimedia (short URLs, lower-thirds, end cards) to drive audiences to more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether to outsource or DIY multimedia production
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to create multimedia in-house or hire specialists based on objectives, resources and required production values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if outsourcing, PR pros should understand quality standards to assess assets before inclusion in a release. Balance budget and production needs against the story’s importance and expected journalist usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do: Focus the story but add flexibility for how it is told
rubrics_metrics.description: Visuals should closely align with the accompanying text (terms, structure, tone) while also being able to stand alone for sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a clear title/subtitle on standalone visuals, narrow the visual scope to convey one core idea, make supporting items visually subordinate, consider separate graphics for similar ideas, and choose the format that best communicates complexity (video for compound concepts, infographics for simple stats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do: Brainstorm and consider all format options
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a wide set of multimedia formats rather than defaulting to one type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formats to consider include: screenshots; visualized quotes; charts and graphs; simple infographics; GIFs and memes; and embeds of social posts, YouTube clips, etc. Use the right format for the message and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t: Force reporters to act like art directors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making journalists resize low-resolution images, hunt for high-res files, or perform heavy editing on supplied multimedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple resolution and format options suitable for article pages and social platforms. Offer easy-to-embed versions (embed code/snippets) so reporters can insert assets with minimal work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t: Force reporters to act like lawyers — respect licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: All multimedia must be owned by you or properly licensed/free to use; do not force journalists to clear copyright issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm rights and supply clear licensing or attribution instructions. When including third-party multimedia, ensure it is cleared and document permissions to remove friction for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do: Make use of free and low-cost multimedia tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage modern, easy-to-use tools and templates to create professional-looking multimedia on limited budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Visual.ly, Easel.ly, Canva, Venngage, Piktochart for infographics; iMovie or Magisto for video. Monitor tool reviews (e.g., CreativeBloq) to discover new options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t: Make anyone strain to hear what’s happening onscreen (audio quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio quality is more important than perfect visuals; if people can’t hear the video, they won’t watch it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always mic people on camera, check sound repeatedly (before, after, and post-take), and provide transcripts or captions for environments where sound may be off. Prioritize clear, audible dialog/voiceover over visual polish when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do: Be the brand enforcer in multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia should reflect the brand’s DNA—colors, fonts, logo placement and tone should be consistent with other assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure visuals won’t look out of place on the client’s site or social channels. Consider end-card links back to business objectives or specific website pages to track engagement and reinforce branding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution: reach is the kingdom — pair multimedia with appropriate platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia only matters if it reaches editors, reporters and influencers; choose distribution platforms that maximize audience and editorial pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-channel news releases and platform-specific formats. Tailor asset sets to the channels favored by target outlets (web, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, YouTube) and supply assets that are easily repurposed for those channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a strong variety of multimedia assets to increase pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering multiple types and angles of multimedia makes a story more usable for different outlets and formats, increasing the likelihood of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a detailed press release plus high-quality photos, short videos, infographics, and embed-ready content. The Grant’s Whisky example showed seven assets led to widespread coverage—variety gives journalists options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for fast turnaround of event-driven assets
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering live events, reporters often need photos and videos within hours; plan workflows to deliver assets quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange staffing and processes so images of nightly winners or event highlights are available to reporters as they file stories. Time-sensitive availability can be decisive for coverage (Royal Canadian Horse Show example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use infographics as 'dashboard' visuals for complex/financial data
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics can distill complex or numeric information into glanceable visuals journalists will use in stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine charts, CEO quotes, and 'Fast Facts' areas to present earnings or performance data in a newspaper/magazine-appropriate layout (CEVA example). Provide both infographic and traditional data formats for different audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make multimedia globally and editorially appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: For multi-region coverage, consider how elements like sound, language, and cultural context affect usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: include videos without spoken language (background music only) for cross-market suitability; provide local-language captions or region-specific graphics when appropriate (LG and OpenTable examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia can tell a complete story if planned and scripted
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-planned video or multimedia package can stand alone to explain complex products or narratives in layman’s terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scripting, storyboarding, and B-roll that together explain technical concepts and business cases clearly (Varian Halcyon example). Design assets to be self-explanatory while linking to deeper resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make multimedia mobile-friendly and shareworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Design assets so they display and perform well on mobile devices and are likely to be shared across social platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create mobile-friendly infographics and region-specific sharable content (e.g., OpenTable’s regional infographics). Consider image sizing, aspect ratios, and concise text for mobile consumption.
